_readme: Session 5's record, written as the work went. Self-contained: it assumes you have read neither the conversation nor the earlier session files. 'verified' means it was run and observed; 'reasoned' means it looks right but was not executed. The handoff entry point is ../MANIFEST.json, and the plan for what comes next is ../manifests/roadmap.json.
session_theme: Pay the debt, then people the valley. The frontend was one 2047-line file holding seven systems; it is five files now. On that footing the valley grew a town, a village and two farmsteads, houses you and the residents walk into, and seven people who keep a daily schedule and talk.

user_intent.the_ask: Started as roadmap session 5: 'look at the manifest for emberforge and start the next section of work' -- the split. Expanded mid-session, twice.
user_intent.expansion_1: 'also make the world bigger and add npc and there houses and make the towna dn village and my house and the mechanics for them'
user_intent.expansion_2: 'continue to amek the manifest json larger and continue to mput new idea in there for more idea for more sessions'
clarifying_answers: Interiors: 'Enter every house' -- real interiors you walk into, the player's bed moves inside the player's house.

World size: no option picked. Verbatim: 'procedraly generated or somthing with genarlly smart rulers idk for know make it normal but later on make it possible to port it to be open world'. Taken to mean: keep it near normal now, but make generation data-driven so an open-world port is a swap, not a rewrite.
Settlements: 'Town + village + farmsteads' -- expanded town, a separate village, and 1-2 lone farmsteads each with a house, a small plot and one NPC.
Sequencing: 'Split first, then build' in the same session, stop-able after the split.

done_this_session.what: Split static/index.html (2047 lines) into world.js, render.js, play.js, ui.js.
done_this_session.note: Classic scripts sharing one global scope, the arrangement audio.js and selftest.js already use -- no import wiring, the move was almost entirely cut-and-paste. index.html keeps the CSS, the DOM, the state object S, the small utilities and the boot sequence (~470 lines). No logic changed in the split itself; the 40-check browser self-test passed unchanged before anything else was touched, which is what separates a refactor from a rewrite.

done_this_session.what: worldgen.py is layout-driven. emberfield/layout.py holds DEFAULT_LAYOUT.
done_this_session.note: A layout is a list of places, each with a kind, a zone (fractions of the world, so it is resolution-independent) and a size. worldgen.place_in_zone scores candidate pads on flatness and dryness and picks the best; _mst_edges wires a minimum spanning tree of roads between the farm, the settlements, the farmsteads and the cave; _drain fills any water or cliff that intrudes on a pad. The renderer and the save format still depend only on the seed, the width, the height and the regions dict -- which is the whole point: a future open-world or chunked generator is a different layout plus a different place_in_zone, nothing downstream.

done_this_session.what: The valley is 128x96 (was 96x72), and holds a farm, a town, a village and two farmsteads.
done_this_session.note: 1.78x the area -- 'normal', modest bake (2048x1536 per palette, three cached). The town has a paved square, the stall, a well and five houses; the village a green with a well and four houses; each farmstead a house, a small worked patch and one resident.

done_this_session.what: Houses you walk into. emberfield/interiors.py, the indoor counterpart to wilds.py.
done_this_session.note: A building carries a door tile and a building id. Pressing space on the door swaps in a small walled room -- generated deterministically from the building id plus the valley seed, never stored, exactly like the wilds. Leaving drops you back on the tile south of the door. A save made indoors describes the valley. The player's house has the bed (session 2's bed, moved inside) with use:'sleep' and a marked corner for session 6's storage and workbench; every other house has a decorative bed, a table and a hearth.

done_this_session.what: NPCs as a content type. 'npcs' added to forge_content.TYPES; seven people seeded.
done_this_session.note: An npc file is a sprite, a home building, a schedule of [hour, place] stops, and a set of canned lines. The frontend builds them when the valley loads, walks them between stops on a real BFS path (a greedy walk wedges a villager behind the first tree), and hides them when they are home. Talking uses the same space-to-interact path as everything else; the shopkeeper opens the stall. They exist only in the valley -- the simulation and the renderer stand down in the wilds and indoors, and S.npcs is left intact so they are where you left them on return.

done_this_session.what: New art: two packs, emberfield-buildings and emberfield-villagers.
done_this_session.note: House sprites for the player, town, village and farmstead; a well, a door mat, a hearth, a table; the wood_floor, interior_wall and rug tiles; three recoloured villager sprite sets built from the player's pose. New packs rather than edits to the existing ones, because the seeder skips packs that already exist -- new sprites in emberfield-nature.json would never have been written.

done_this_session.what: 25 new Python tests (120 total) and 9 new browser self-tests (49 total). All passing.
done_this_session.note: Python: settlement and farmstead reachability across a seed sweep; every building door walkable and reachable; every interior deterministic and fully walkable with its exit reachable from spawn; only the player interior has a sleepable bed; every NPC names a real home, sprite and schedule stop; every villager sprite set exists. Browser: entering a house keeps your pack and crops; a save made indoors names the valley; stepping out puts you by the door; every NPC can path home-to-stop; talking returns a line; the shopkeeper opens the stall; nobody lives on ground the night would spawn a foe on.

not_done_yet: Crafting, skills, tool upgrades, and the storage chest in the player's house -- session 6. The player interior leaves a marked corner (regions['storage_spot']) for it. This is where the next session starts.
NPC relationships, gifts, affection; model-driven NPC dialogue -- session 8.
The path tile still reads almost the same brown as tilled soil, so a paved town square looks muddy. Carried from every previous session; now more visible because there is a lot more paving.
Shoreline and cliff autotiling; music; a dodge roll.
The open-world / chunked port itself -- session 5 only made generation portable to it.

assessment.what_went_well: The split paid for itself immediately: NPCs and interiors touch rendering, simulation, interaction and content at once, and landing them in four focused files instead of one 2600-line one was the difference between the session finishing and not. The layout refactor also paid off -- adding the village and the farmsteads was a line each in DEFAULT_LAYOUT plus a kind branch, exactly the shape the project is built for. And interiors reused the wilds' park-and-swap wholesale; enterBuilding is enterWilds with a different fetch.
what_i_got_wrong: Fenced the farm inside _lay_farm, before the path network existed, so the fence left no gate and the farm was sealed. Moved fencing back to after the roads are carved.

Put the farm's zone in the wettest corner of the map (the shore is designed to land there), so the placement search could not find a dry pad and fell back to one full of water that walled the plot off from its own gate. Fixed by scoring pads softly with a heavy water/cliff penalty rather than hard-rejecting, and by draining any water left under a settlement.

The frontend's object index buckets a house onto its own doorstep tile (floor-based, inclusive) even though the collision ellipse does not reach it, so the NPC path finder read every route to a door as blocked. Changed tileBlocked to sample the real pixel collision at the tile centre instead of trusting the bucket.

resolvePlace returned the stall's and the well's own tiles, which are solid, so NPCs could never path 'to the stall'. Added walkableNear to resolve a landmark to the nearest tile you can actually stand on.

The first pass of the wood_floor and interior_wall tiles were both brown noise -- indistinguishable, so a rendered room had no visible edge. Redrew the floor as warm plank courses and the wall as pale plaster with dark studs; also the ?demo=house helper was handing enterBuilding a regions.buildings registry entry (no .building field) instead of the door object, so it silently no-op'd. Both fixed while closing the 'interior unseen' gap -- the room now renders legibly and has been screenshotted (s6-interior, s6-npc).
risks: Seven NPCs each recompute a BFS path when their schedule stop changes -- a few times an in-game day, on a 128x96 grid, so cheap. But nobody has watched them for a full day at normal speed; a schedule that sends someone across the whole valley every few hours would have them permanently in transit.

The valley got bigger and gained ~10 houses, a well per settlement and seven walking actors, none of it profiled on the actual machine. The bake is one more 12 MB canvas; the per-frame cost is seven extra depth-sorted sprites. Reasoned to be fine, not measured.

The town square and every settlement's paving still reads as mud -- the path tile is nearly the same brown as tilled soil, and there is a lot more paving now. It is the first item in the roadmap backlog.

decision_record._why: One scoped instruction, two mid-session expansions, and four clarifying answers. The rest were judgement calls, recorded so a later session can disagree.

taken_without_asking.decision: Kept classic scripts for the split rather than moving to ES modules.
taken_without_asking.why: audio.js and selftest.js are already classic scripts on a shared global scope. Modules would mean an export/import edit at every one of a few hundred cross-references -- risk with no payoff, when the self-test is the safety net and it only works if the move is mechanical.

taken_without_asking.decision: Modest size bump to 128x96, not bigger.
taken_without_asking.why: The user said 'make it normal for now'. The value of the session was the layout refactor that makes size a parameter, not the size itself.

taken_without_asking.decision: NPC houses are not walked by their residents -- an NPC at home is simply hidden, shown at the door otherwise.
taken_without_asking.why: Pathing an NPC through a door into a second map and back is a lot of machinery for something you would rarely see. 'They went inside' is enough, and the interior is still there for the player to enter.

taken_without_asking.decision: A villager's bed is a decorative sprite with no 'use'; only the player's bed sleeps.
taken_without_asking.why: Sleeping in a stranger's bed to end your day is a bug you would file. The bed sprite still dresses the room.

taken_without_asking.decision: Landmarks in a schedule ('stall', 'well') resolve to the nearest walkable tile, not the object's own tile.
taken_without_asking.why: You stand next to a stall, not on it. The alternative -- a separate 'approach' field on every landmark -- is data the geometry already implies.

verification_status.browser_selftest: 49 passed (40 from session 4, 9 new). Run: http://127.0.0.1:8434/?seed=777&selftest=1 then GET /api/selftest.

Performance on the actual laptop with the larger bake and seven actors.

conventions_this_session_adds: A settlement is one entry in emberfield/layout.py DEFAULT_LAYOUT plus a kind branch in worldgen._lay_place. Zones are fractions of the world, never tile coordinates.
worldgen.place_in_zone is the seam an open-world port replaces. Nothing else should learn the map's size -- the renderer, the save and the frontend all read only seed, width, height and regions.
A house interior is generated from its building id plus the valley seed and never stored, exactly like a wilds cavern. interiors.py is its own file; do not fold it into worldgen.
An NPC is one JSON file in ~/ForgeGameData/npcs. home is a building id; schedule stops are region names, landmark names, building ids or [x, y]; the game paths them there.
New sprites go in a new art pack, never appended to an existing pack file -- the seeder skips packs that already exist, so an append is silently lost until --force.
